summary: Virginia-born US Army officer Robert E. Lee had enslaved people at Arlington whipped, broke his oath to lead Confederate armies to defeat in the Civil War, and after 1865 opposed civil rights for freed Black Americans.

evidence.note: Father Henry Lee III finishes law school in 1773, then a long segment on his Revolutionary War career
Lee born January 1807 at Stratford Hall
Father-in-law Custis dies in 1857; Lee takes over Arlington and hires out enslaved people to pay debts
Lee orders recaptured escapees stripped and lashed; press report says he whipped Mary Norris himself
Lee's letters show casual racism, including a slur
Whole part covers his decision to break his oath and join the secessionist rebellion
Lost Cause portrayals, from a children's biography onward, recur through every part
Lee made commander of Virginia's forces in Richmond before joining the Confederacy
Long assessment of his generalship as Confederate war leader, through Gettysburg and surrender
After the war Lee lobbies against laws protecting freed Black Americans
Lee dies in October 1870 after a stroke
2017 newspaper column defending Lee shows the myth still active today

notes: Covered span starts 1773 with father Light-Horse Harry's career (secondary subject, most of part 1); Norman-era and colonial family lore treated as background. Mexican-American War (MX) and Cortina raids get only a few minutes, so MX left out of setting. propaganda-media chosen for Lost Cause myth-making; no closer theme for historical memory or memorialisation. Secession tagged coups-insurrections.
